title: Reversible vs single-sided blackwork
subtitle: Holbein stitch for both sides; back stitch for the front only
excerpt: Traditional blackwork was reversible, worked so the back of the cloth looked as clean as the front. Modern blackwork often uses back stitch and is worked for the front only. Both are valid approaches; the choice shapes which stitch path you use.
sourceNotes: Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882). Weldon's Practical Needlework (1880s to 1900s), blackwork sampler instructions.

glossaryTerms.definition: Double-running stitch worked along a counted path so the thread looks identical on both sides of the fabric. The traditional outline stitch for reversible blackwork.
A stitch worked by bringing the needle up one stitch length ahead, then inserting it back at the end of the previous stitch. Forms a solid line; single-pass, not reversible.

content.text: The difference between reversible and single-sided blackwork comes down to one choice:

Reversible blackwork is appropriate when both sides of the cloth are visible: on clothing edges, collars, cuffs, and detached borders where the fabric turns and shows the back. It is also the historically correct approach for embroidery on garments, where the black thread must look the same from inside and outside the collar.
Framed work, cushions, and items with a lining do not need reversibility. Single-sided back stitch is faster and covers ground more quickly.
The Holbein stitch path for reversible work

Plan the path of each line before stitching. A reversible fill pattern needs a continuous path that can be worked as a running stitch out and a filling running stitch back, without any section requiring a back-stitch overlap.
Work the first pass as an even running stitch along each line. Leave a gap between each stitch equal to the length of the stitch itself.
Return along the same path, filling every gap. Enter the same holes the first pass used; do not create new holes beside the existing ones.
The back stitch path for single-sided work
Bring the needle up one stitch length ahead of the start of the line.
Insert the needle at the start of the line (going backwards), and bring it up one stitch length further ahead.
Continue, always inserting one stitch back and emerging one stitch ahead. Back stitch is faster than Holbein stitch but leaves an irregular knot on the back of the cloth.
If you are unsure which to use, look at the finished piece. Will anyone ever see the back? If the answer is no, back stitch is fine. If the answer is possibly, use
and the question will not matter.
